analytic.title: Reaching Optimum Solutions for the Low Power Hard Real-Time Task Allocation on Multiple Heterogeneous Processors Problem

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The usage of heterogeneous multicore platforms is appealing for applications, e.g. hard real-time systems, due to the potential reduced energy consumption offered by such platforms. However, the power wall is still a barrier to improving the processor design process due to the power consumption of components. Hard real-time systems are part of life critical environments and reducing the energy consumption on such systems is an onerous and complex process. This paper assesses the problem of finding optimum allocations and frequency assignments of hard realtime tasks among heterogeneous processors targeting low power consumption but taking into account timing constraints. We also propose models based on a well-established formulation in the operational research literature of the Multilevel Generalized Assignment Problem (MGAP). We tackle the problem from the perspective of different integer programming mathematical formulations and their interplay on the search for optimal solutions for RM and EDF. Computational experiments show that providing upper bounds determined by a meta-heuristic based on genetic algorithm reduces the time to finding optimal solution from hours to milliseconds, enabling us to still pursue optimum in larger instances.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The power wall is a barrier to improvement in the processor design process due to the power consumption of components. Power consumption has become the primary influence in overall microprocessor design complexity [1] due to ideal geometric scaling and non-ideal electrical scaling. It is no longer viable to simply increase clock speeds of existing designs [2]. Power consumption is a major aspect that limits the performance of computers in different sides of the computing spectrum. The pursuit of energy efficiency is useful for mobile devices to improve operating duration and also helpful for server systems to reduce power bills [3].

Modern computing systems often adopt multiple processing elements to enhance the computing capability and reduce the power consumption, especially for embedded systems [3]. Besides, modern multicore processors for the embedded market are often heterogeneous in nature [4]. Therefore, the heterogeneous multicore platforms have become the de-facto solution to cope with the rapid increase of system complexity, reliability, and energy consumption [5].

Practitioners execute applications with hard deadline restrictions on multiple heterogeneous processors due to the expected energy consumption reduction. Nevertheless, developing software with timing constraints for multiple heterogeneous processors is a complex task. Scheduling becomes especially hard to deal with, particularly under low power constraints. Our approach aims at life-critical hard real-time systems such as Unmanned Aerial Vehicles, Control system in the automotive area, and distributed computing under severe constraints, e.g., tracking and target monitoring, military, and environmental remote monitoring.

The Multilevel Generalized Assignment Problem (MGAP) consists of minimizing the assignment cost of a set of jobs to machines, each having associated therewith a capacity constraint. Each machine can perform a job with different performance states that entail different costs and amount of resources required. The MGAP is originally in the context of large manufacturing systems as a more general variant of the well-known Generalized Assignment Problem (GAP) [6]. In this paper, we correlate MGAP model with the problem of assigning frequencies and distributing hard-real time tasks on heterogeneous processors minimizing energy consumption.

Nowadays processors may be seen as machines with several performance states due to Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) technique. DVFS is a well established power reduction strategy and it has already been a research topic for decades. The premises are the variation of processors' workloads and the quadratic relationship between energy consumption and voltage [7]. The energy consumption depends on dynamic and static energy [1].

Therefore, the problem we are addressing in this paper is: How to find optimum hard real-time tasks distribution among heterogeneous processors respecting timing constraints and targeting low power consumption? The contributions of this work are: (i) the usage of classical MGAP model on this problem that delivers (ii) optimum hard real-time task allocation and optimum frequency to task assignment, (iii) with system energy consumption minimization for (iv) different scheduling policies. The results we present on this research question focus on solving the problem optimally on practical instances sizes. Effective methods support reducing power bills, improve system reliability, and increase the efficient usage of energy; last but not least, assisting to reduce environmental impacts.

The organization of this paper is as follows. The processor model and task model are defined in Section II. Formulations for different scheduling policies and a model growth analysis are discussed in Section III. We describe the implementation of solvers and of a genetic algorithm in Section IV. Computational experiments are detailed in Section V. We compare our results with existing literature in Section VI. Section VII closes this paper with final comments and future work.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODELS
div.p: The processor model resembles a Multi-Processor System-On-Chip (MPSoC) architecture, such as Exynos 5 Octa [8]. The system is composed by a set of m processors, H 1 , H 2 , . . . , H m . Each core may operate on l different performance states, 1 ≤ k ≤ l. The frequency of performance state k is F (k) and the power consumption is P (k). The idle power of processor i is P idle,i .

Our proposal can be used with no extra effort on other architectures. We have exercised on multiple heterogeneous clusters [9]. Due to text size limitation, we focus on a platform with m processors with same performance states, but still heterogeneous in terms of instruction set, i.e. same task has different code size and execution time for different processors.

In the remaining sections of this paper we adopt the following notation. A task model M is a set composed by n tasks τ j . A task τ j ∈ M, with j ≤ n, has the properties: fixed priority p j ; worst-case execution cycle W CEC j ; worstcase execution time C j (f ), which is a function of frequency f , thus C j (f ) =

div.head: III. MODELS FOR DIFFERENT SCHEDULING POLICIES
A. MGAP Model
div.p: Considering the problem characteristics and the set of frequencies of each processor as machine levels, we propose to use the MGAP integer programming mathematical formulation. The classical MGAP formulation is in Equation 1.

This formulation applies each task deadline as a constraint against their response time in the linear programming. We are not considering precedence or mutual exclusion at this work. div.head: E. Analysis on Formulations
div.p: The previous mathematical formulations are similar in the sense of growth. They all have a tri-indexed decision variable. Also, the number of variables increases with the number of machines, number of tasks, and the number of performance states. They share similar growth of number of constraints, which increases with the number of machines and tasks, with the exception of RM RESP, whose constrains increases quadratically with the number of tasks.

The constraints of RM RESP and RM UTIL, however, are harder to implement. Each θ i in these formulations is dependent on the decision variable, i.e. on the assignment and task distribution. Because the exponents of the decision variables are different than one in these constraints, these are Non-Linear Programming (NLP) formulations. MGAP and EDF UTIL are Linear Programming (LP) formulations. Table I summarizes characteristics of these formulations.

div.head: IV. IMPLEMENTATIONS A. Solvers: Finding Optimum Solutions
div.p: We wrote an implementation of the previous models using C++ CPLEX Concert [13] to create a solver for each of them [14]. The solver's input is a configuration file containing the processing model, its power model, and the desired task model. Each solver outputs a boolean, informing if a feasible, and therefore schedulable, solution is found. Also, when the input has feasible solutions, the solver outputs the distribution of hard real-time tasks among the processors that consumes less power among the possible assignments, informing as well in which frequency each tasks may be executed. When asked, the solver may also output the execution time.

In the implementation of these solvers, we configure Concert to sustain reproducibility. We have limited the amount of threads to one (IloCplex::Threads = 1). The workable memory is set to 1 GB (IloCplex::WorkMem = 1024). The solver tree is restricted to 2 GB (IloCplex::TreLim = 2048). We also configured Concert to be deterministic (IloCplex::Param::Parallel = 1).

div.head: B. Approximation by Means of Genetic Algorithm (GA)
div.p: We also wrote a genetic algorithm (GA) for each mathematical model [14]. We follow a similar approach as existing in the literature for other formulations on this problem [15]. In our GA implementation, the DNA is a sequence of 0's and 1's and each gene represent one of the elements of the tridimensional decision variable of the mathematical model. The algorithm can be simplified into four steps.

Initialization: we initially random-generate 5000 individuals. If none of them is a feasible solution, we return the empty set ∅. If we find less than 50 feasible individuals, then we return the one with highest fitness. But when we find 50 feasible individuals, we repeat the following steps for a maximum of 100 generations, or 10 generations with same best fitness, and return the individual with best fitness.
Elitism: we include the individual with best fitness in the next generation. We always keep the best individual and insert it in the next generation.

Selection: we execute a tournament in the current population. Only 5 individuals, randomly selected, participate in the tournament. The winner of the tournament is the individual with best fitness among those participating of it.

Crossover: we insert in the next generation the result of a crossover between winners of two tournaments. The crossover operation between individuals I 1 and I 2 is done by means of selecting a pivot gene p. The genes lower than p are copied from I 1 , the remaining genes are copied from I 2 . When resulting individual is not feasible, we return I 1 , if fitness(I 1 ) > fitness(I 2 ), or I 2 otherwise.

Notes: All generated generations are composed by feasible individuals only. Thus, we decided to avoid the mutation operator because adding it increases the simulation time as it requires checking if the individual is still valid after mutation.

div.head: V. COMPUTATIONAL EXPERIMENTS A. Experiment Design
div.p: The objective of this computational experiment is to evaluate the model in terms of performance, objective function, and execution time. The performance of each solver is determined by the amount of valid solutions it is able to find for a given input. The evaluation of solver's objective function aims to understand the ability to reduce energy consumption for a given input. Finally, the execution time is measured to compare the impact on project design phase. We estimate the execution time of each solver using wall clock. The machine used to perform the simulation experiments has an AMD FX TM -9370, 8 cores executed at 1.4 GHz. We use Debian GNU/Linux 8.2 with 32 GB of DDR3 memory executed at 1.33 GHz.

We use random-generated task models. We vary number of tasks in each random-generated models between 5, 10, 15, and 20. We vary the total system utilization between 10%, 20%, 30%, 40%, 50%, and 60%. The total system utilization is estimated using the highest frequency available, but final total system utilization is determined by the solution given by the solver. The tasks WCEC is uniformly distributed between 50 000 and 100 000 cycles, but a task may have a different amount of cycles for each processor, representing their difference in instruction set. We chose to have tasks periods uniformly distributed between three sets: large period, medium period, and short period. When a task has a large period, its period is chosen from a normally distributed value between 100ms and 1000ms. Similarly, a medium period is normally distributed between 10ms and 100ms, and a short period is normally distributed between 1ms and 10ms. We chose to make deadlines equal to periods and to disregard precedence and shared resources to perform a fair comparison among policies.

Our experiment considers a target platform of four processors. Processors are based on XScale processors [16]. Each processor may operate at 624 MHz, 520 MHz, 416 MHz, 312 MHz, or 208 MHz. The idle power consumption is 260 mW. The energy consumption is estimated for the duration of the LCM of tasks' periods, as in the objective function of each model.

The result of the execution of GA is used as input of a second execution of each solver. The data of all executions on each instance is available for download in a public repository [14], but we present only the summary of them in the following sections, due to text space limitations.

div.head: B. Results
div.p: The search for optimum solutions using the solvers of each model found only feasible, but not optimum, solutions. In several cases, we reached the time limit of 30 min. We can also confirm this observation by looking at the difference between the lower and upper bounds at the end of execution of each solver (GAP). Table II lists the average of the executions of each combination of number tasks and total system utilization (U total ). We call special attention to the RM UTIL results in these experiments. For example, for 20 tasks and 40 % of total system utilization, the average GAP was 32.86 %, and the RM UTIL solver always reached the time limit of 30 min.

We, then, have executed the Genetic Algorithm (GA) on every instance with feasible solutions. The GA produces a feasible solution, typically non-optimal. However, the solution provisioned by the GA can be used as an upper-bound to solvers in the search for optimum solutions. Therefore, we re-executed each solver on each instance, but using the upperbound and initial solution produced by the GAs.

The results for RM RESP are listed in Table III, which groups the execution of each instance per number of tasks and total system utilization. Using GA in RM RESP reduced, for example, the execution time from 30 min to less than 2 min in the case of 20 tasks and 50 % of total system utilization, while still reducing the total system energy consumption.
For these instances, we observed a higher improvement while applying the GA output as input to the solver RM UTIL. Table IV lists the results for RM UTIL using the GA as input.

In Table IV, we also group the execution of each instance per number of tasks and total system utilization, and present the average on each column. In all cases in which the GAP for RM UTIL was significant, using the GA inputs made the RM UTIL to reach a GAP of either 0.00 or 0.01. Also, the GA inputs reduced, for example, the execution time from 30 min to less than 1 min in the case of 20 tasks and 60 % or total system utilization, while still reducing the total system energy.

The improvement for EDF UTIL are less apparent as this solver already had a small GAP. However, in some cases we still see an improvement in execution time. The results of using GA output in the solver EDF UTIL are listed in Table V. We also highlight the cases that the execution of GA alone produced a solution with lower power consumption in a shorter execution. For example, for 20 tasks and 50 %, the GA produced solutions in less than 1 min with total system energy lower than the solutions found by the solver in 30 min.

div.head: C. Targeting Larger Instances
div.p: We exercised the strategy of providing upper bounds to solvers on larger instances. We have random-generated three instances with 50 tasks. These instances are designed to have 60 % of total system utilization if all processors are kept at the maximum speed, to achieve a fair comparison between all scheduling policies, avoiding crossing their theoretical limits. The results are listed on Table VI, VII, and VIII, which list the average value of 4 execution on the same instance.

Table VI shows the results of RM RESP executed on the larger instances. On the one hand, we observed that on all three instances the solver alone is not able to produce any results due to memory limitations. The GA, on the other hand, is able to find a feasible solution in less than 10 s. For the instances 'asbke0DO' and 'qNnTqt2P', the solver could find another feasible solution with lower power consumption in less than 45 min when fed with GA solution and upper bound, but with a GAP of 11.16 %. On instance '5HPzJAru', however, the RM RESP solver was able to find the optimum solution in less than one second.

We see a similar pattern for RM UTIL. Table VII presents the results of RM UTIL executed on the larger instances. Similar to RM RESP, we observed that on all threes instances the solver alone is not able to produce any results due to memory limitations. The GA is able to produce a feasible solution in less than 1 min. The optimum solution was also found by RM UTIL for instance '5HPzJAru' in less than one second when the GA solution and upper bounds were used as input. On instances 'asbke0DO' and 'qNnTqt2P', the solver is able to find a feasible solution in less than 45 min, using a GA solution and upper bound, with GAP of 32.51 %.

Table VIII depicts the results of EDF UTIL executed on the larger instances. Here, the solver is able to find the optimum solution alone in less than two seconds on all instances. The GA also is able to find a feasible solution in less than two seconds. Feeding GA solution and upper bound helps the solver only in finding the optimum solution faster.

div.head: VI. RELATED WORK AND DISCUSSION OF RESULTS
div.p: The interplay between different schedulability analyses and integer programming mathematical formulation have influence on the performance of solvers while searching for the optimum solution. Providing upper bounds and initial feasible solutions may accelerate the search process. We also observe that, while targeting optimum solutions, using strict constraints may reduce overall system energy consumption [9].

In the literature, there are strategies to determine hard real-time task distribution in heterogeneous platforms. Their approach typically focus on either heuristics or approximation algorithms [3]. There are also models proposed to cover optimal solutions that minimize the energy consumption of hard real-time systems with multiple heterogeneous processors. The typical formulation is a 0/1 integer linear programming model which considers a continuous processor frequency domain and determines a single operating frequency per processor [3], [4], [5], [17], [18]. However, using the MGAP model is a better fit to this problem because practical processors still use a discrete set of frequencies [19].

The adoption of DVFS is common in optimization procedures, such as task allocation, and frequency to task assignment. The aim is to find optimal energy-aware scheduling on heterogeneous platforms while considering individual task deadlines [3]. Overall system energy reduction is due to workload split and to frequency minimization to meet tasks deadlines. Adoption of the well-known utilization based schedulability analyses is common [3], [4], [5], [15], [17], [18], [20], [21], [22], [23], [24]. The simplification on the model and on the solving process as using utilization constraints produces formulations similar to the multiple knapsack problem. We confirm these efforts with EDF UTIL solver, the fastest in our experiments. However, our work also propose formulations for different scheduling polices for practical processors.

For the classic MGAP there are extreme fast algorithms. MGAP problem instances are solvable up to hundreds of machines with tens of speed levels, to map hundreds of tasks. For example, Osorio and Laguna [25] proposed a Branch-and-Cut algorithm in 2003 and were able to solve instances up to 60 tasks, 30 machines, and two speed levels. Ceselli and Righini [26], in 2006, proposed a Branch-and-Price strategy, solving up to 400 tasks, 80 machines and five levels. Another Branch-and-Cut algorithm proposed by Avella et al. in 2013 [27] can solve 200 tasks, 30 machines and five levels, for specific problem instances. We contribute with the present work with a new application of the MGAP model.

div.head: VII. FINAL REMARKS
div.p: In this paper we assess the problem of how to find optimum hard real-time tasks distribution among heterogeneous processors respecting timing constraints and minimizing low power consumption. Our study focus on optimum solutions after reviewing the existing models.

We proposed the usage of a well-known classical combinatorial optimization problem, MGAP, to represent the characteristics and constraints of the problem. We first used MGAP to model systems using EDF (D j = T j ), which represents the existing models in the literature. We also extended the proposed MGAP to derive extra models considering utilization bounds for RM (D j = T j ) and response time analysis for RM (D j = T j ) and DM (D j ≤ T j ) scheduling policies. The implementation of such models delivers optimum hard real-time task allocation and optimum frequency to task assignment minimizing system energy consumption. Based on our experimental results we recommend for static priority policies the usage of MGAP response time based model. The MGAP response time based model, implemented for RM in our experiments, finds configurations with the same energy consumption as the literature EDF representation, but with an execution time penalty.

We recognize that targeting optimal solutions for this problem is not a simple task, specially considering the fast growth of its formulations. However, the optimum is still reachable in some instances, as shown in our computational experiment, by applying well-known combinatorial optimization techniques. For example, we have exercised the usage of a GA to find upper bounds and initial feasible solutions, boosting the search for the optimal while executing solvers.

As future works, we will investigate different algorithms for MGAP applied on the problem of assigning hard realtime tasks among heterogeneous processors with different performance state. We believe that combining the response time analysis with the existing algorithms may produce faster solvers for this problem. We also understand the theoretical limitations of RM and DM policies, however, the usage of response time analysis in 0/1 integer linear programming models presented in this paper can be used as baseline enabling further studies on precedence and mutual exclusion constraints.
